prompt.context: Your client is a car insurance company. Their claims processing department is under pressure to reduce costs.
prompt.question: How might you help them reduce claims processing costs?

clarifying_info.q: What is driving the cost reduction pressure?
clarifying_info.a: The CEO believes competitors' claims processing cost is less — not necessarily the overall payout, but the actual processing itself is cheaper.

exhibits.title: Cost Structure Table
exhibits.shows: A table with two columns: Previous Costs and Proposed Costs (blank). Rows are: Revenues, Phase A, Phase B, Payouts, Profits.

framework: Understand the current claims processing workflow (Phase A and Phase B) and compare to competitor process
Identify where cost differences arise — specifically time spent per claim in each phase
Quantify efficiency: how many claims can an inspector process per day (travel time, inspection time, report writing time, total hours worked)
Assess whether adopting the competitor process model for Phase B reduces cost
Evaluate risks associated with switching to the competitor model
Form a recommendation with a pilot program to validate impact before full rollout

questions.prompt: Walk through the client's claims processing workflow and compare it to the competitor's workflow.
questions.guidance: Client Phase A (same for all): call center receives call; agent assigns inspector and informs customer; inspector visits damaged car; inspector prepares report and estimates payout. Client Phase B (our process): inspector physically visits the car. Competitor Phase B: customer is instructed to get three mechanic quotes and fax them in; agents review quotes using a proprietary system and decide reward amount (not necessarily lowest). The key difference is that the client uses physical inspector visits in Phase B while the competitor shifts the legwork to the customer.

questions.prompt: Calculate how efficient each operation is — how many claims can an inspector process in a day?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up time per claim including: travel time to/from damaged car, time to physically inspect the car, time to write the report and estimate payout. Sum these to get total time per claim, then divide the total work hours in a day to find claims per inspector per day. Candidate should surface that travel time is the primary driver making the client's process more time-intensive than the competitor's model.

math.setup: Assume an 8-hour workday. Let travel time per claim = T_travel, inspection time = T_inspect, report writing time = T_report. Claims per day = 480 min / (T_travel + T_inspect + T_report). Candidate is expected to draw their own assumptions for each component.
steps: Assign reasonable assumptions (e.g., travel 60 min round-trip, inspection 30 min, report 30 min = 120 min per claim)
Claims per day = 480 / 120 = 4 claims per inspector per day
Compare to competitor model where inspector time is replaced by reviewing faxed quotes (much less travel, perhaps 15-20 min per claim) → potentially 24 claims per agent-day
math.answer: Illustrative: client processes ~4 claims/inspector/day vs competitor ~24 claims/agent-day due to elimination of travel; exact numbers depend on candidate assumptions

questions.prompt: Complete the Proposed Costs column in the exhibit and explain your assumptions.
questions.guidance: Phase A costs stay the same because Phase A is identical across companies. Phase B costs decrease because inspector travel is eliminated and replaced by quote review. Payouts are variable — they could go up or down depending on how the proprietary quote review system performs. Profits are therefore also variable. A strong candidate flags that payouts are uncertain and may rise or fall.

math.setup: Previous: Revenues=100, Phase A=10, Phase B=20, Payouts=60, Profits=10. Proposed changes: Phase A unchanged at 10; Phase B reduced (competitor model eliminates inspector travel); Payouts variable; Profits variable.
steps: Phase B: 10 (reduced, e.g., cutting travel costs roughly in half or more)
Payouts: 70 (variable — may drift; casebook shows 70 as illustrative but flags uncertainty)
math.answer: Proposed: Revenues=100, Phase A=10 (same), Phase B=10 (something less, e.g. ~10), Payouts=70 (variable), Profits=10 (variable)

brainstorming.prompt: What risks are associated with switching to the competitor's Phase B process?

categories.name: Fraud risk
ideas: Customers sourcing their own mechanic quotes creates opportunity for collusion between customer and mechanics
Inflated quotes could increase payouts unexpectedly
Proprietary review system may not catch all fraudulent quotes

categories.name: Payout uncertainty
ideas: Payout amounts may drift upward or downward in unpredictable ways
Removing inspector control over estimates reduces standardization
Three-quote model does not guarantee lowest cost — client pays 'reasonable' amount, not minimum

categories.name: Customer experience
ideas: Some customers (especially serious accident victims) prefer the ease of a scheduled inspector visit rather than sourcing their own quotes
Forcing customers to do legwork may reduce satisfaction
Customers purchase insurance on price not processing convenience, but post-accident experience still affects retention

categories.name: Operational transition
ideas: Staff retraining required — agents need to use the proprietary quote-review system
Inspector workforce reduction may involve severance and morale issues
IT and systems investment needed to implement proprietary review platform

recommendation: Adopt the competitor's Phase B model (customer-sourced mechanic quotes reviewed by a proprietary system) to reduce processing costs by eliminating inspector travel time
Phase B processing costs could be reduced by approximately 50% or more; overall profitability impact depends on payout movement
risks: Payout amounts are uncertain and may drift up or down with the new model
Fraud risk increases if the proprietary review system is not robust
Some customers may respond negatively to being required to source their own quotes
next_steps: Survey a selection of the client base (and potential clients) anonymously to gauge acceptance of the new model
Institute a pilot program in a select geographic area to measure the effect on payout levels and customer satisfaction
If pilot results are positive on both cost and customer morale, roll out system-wide
